amiable

/AY-mee-uh-buhl/ - the stress falls on AY · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Amiable means good-natured and pleasant.

The amiable crossing guard has a kind word for every student, and even motorists stuck at her stop sign end up smiling.

Example

Camp reviews mention the food, the lake, and — every single year — Cookie, the amiable head cook who hums while he serves, teases gently, and sends homesick first-timers back to their cabins feeling like regulars.

Amiable praises a person's overall good nature: pleasant, kind, easy to be around. It is broader than a single friendly act — one warm handshake doesn't make someone amiable; a steady, good-natured way with people does.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

good-natured: Good-natured describes a kindly, even temperament — someone slow to anger and quick to help. Amiable covers that kindness and adds pleasantness as company: an amiable person is not just kind inside but easy and agreeable to be around. Good-natured points at disposition; amiable points at how the company feels.

likable: Likable only says people take to someone, for any reason at all — talent, humor, good looks. Amiable names one particular reason: a steady, pleasant good nature that makes a person easy company. A brilliant but prickly performer can be likable; amiable requires the warmth.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

grumpy: habitually irritable and complaining

sour: resentful and unfriendly in temper

Where it sits · how much the company brightens your mood

pleasant → amiable → delightful

pleasant vs. amiable: Pleasant is milder than amiable — a pleasant clerk gives you no reason to complain, while an amiable one leaves you in a better mood than he found you.

delightful vs. amiable: Delightful goes further than amiable — delightful company is a highlight you talk about afterward, while amiable good nature is steady, comfortable, and everyday.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — ami-: friend, love (Latin amare, amicus)

Suffix — -able: able, worthy of

Put it together: Ami- ('friend,' from Latin amare, 'to love') + -able ('worthy of') = worthy of friendship. Amiable came through Old French from Late Latin amicabilis — the very same ancestor as amicable — and it still describes the person whose good nature makes friendship come naturally.

Use the root in a new word: amity: The reunion's closing toast was, as it is every year, 'to amity.'

Word Choice

neutral / everyday-warm

Amiable praises overall good nature — pleasant, kind, easy company. Affable (also in this unit) narrows that warmth to easy conversation, and amicable describes dealings between potential rivals, not a personality. Say an amiable colleague, an affable interviewer, an amicable settlement.
